source.title: Neural networks memorise personal information from one sample
source.authors: J. Hartley; Pedro P. Sanchez; Fasih Haider; S. Tsaftaris

record.tranche_reason: The study measures memorization of artificially inserted unique features and their effects on predictions; it does not test the claim versions about natural-label generalization, nor the training-error/test-error gap they specify.
record.gate_note: The paper reports unique-feature memorization scores and prediction effects, not results on random-label fitting or the listed generalization measures. Its comparisons of regularization strategies concern M scores, not held-out error, so they do not test V6.
record.test_reason: The study measures sensitivity to a feature inserted into one training example, rather than any outcome specified by V1–V8. Its dropout comparisons report maximum M scores, not held-out error. Figure 4 reports test accuracy during training but does not compare random and natural labels or any other manipulation required by the versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that singly occurring unique features can be memorized early, persist under the tested regularization strategies, and affect predictions. They also demonstrate auditing with restricted data access and discuss robustness and potential privacy risks; they do not demonstrate recovery of an unknown patient's name.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains classifiers on natural-label datasets with one artificially inserted unique feature and measures sensitivity to that feature; it does not test random-label memorization or the claim's training-test generalization outcomes.
record.method_sensitivity: The proportion of memorizing networks differs between the toy setting with a unique z feature and the setting with added z-axis Gaussian noise.

fits_no_version.finding: Statistically significant sensitivity to a singly occurring inserted feature appears in 20%–80% of networks across the Table 2 settings.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Classification networks can memorize a feature occurring in only one training example, with substantial variation across training runs and settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Nonzero maximum M scores remain with dropout, augmentation, weight decay, and batch normalization. The authors state that regularization does not significantly reduce M scores, although Table 3 supplies no unregularized baseline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The tested regularization strategies do not eliminate unique-feature memorization.

fits_no_version.finding: In separate 500-run toy experiments, memorization occurs in 82.6% of networks with an otherwise unused z dimension and 41.4% with Gaussian noise along that dimension; Figure 4 shows memorization from the first epoch.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unique-feature memorization can begin early and is more frequent when the feature also introduces a rare concept.

record.problems: The main measure is a proxy for unique-feature memorization rather than a generalization gap. The study says memorization is not always present and varies with training seeds and stochasticity. Some outcomes are shown only in figures without numerical values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Figure-only findings without described numerical outcomes were not entered as numerical rows.

untested.parts: Near-perfect random-label fitting alongside natural-label generalization and chance-level random-label held-out accuracy.
Held-out error as width increases beyond zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected held-out performance and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD held-out performance under specified tuning budgets.
Batch-size effects on held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Dropout's effect on held-out error, small-data behavior, underfitting, and joint removal with weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization gaps, and comparisons with other measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: All recorded numerical values match Tables 2–3. The M-score baseline is the model's confidence on corresponding clean inputs; Table 3 does not provide a no-regularization baseline. E3 should not be linked to R1: 82.6% is from the separate 500-run rare-concept experiment, whereas R1 records Table 2's 65% across 1000 runs. The study's Methods names MLP-2 for regularization experiments, but Table 3 identifies MLP-1, as the rows correctly report.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out accuracy on natural labels.
Width sweeps and test error beyond the interpolation threshold.
Adaptive optimizer comparisons on held-out performance.
Whether dropout lowers held-out error or underfits; the study measures unique-feature M scores instead.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to the training-test gap.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring the resulting test accuracy.
